title: Curl
body:
How much a [[Vector Field]] is rotating at a point. Input a vector field, output a **vector**: it
has to be, because in three dimensions a rotation needs an axis as well as a rate.

$$
\operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F} = \nabla \times \mathbf{F} =
\begin{vmatrix}
\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\
\partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \\
P & Q & R
\end{vmatrix}
$$

Computed as a cross product, so it is the same symbolic [[Determinant]] expansion used in
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA]], with derivative operators in the middle row. In two dimensions only the
$\mathbf{k}$ component survives and people write the scalar $Q_x - P_y$, which is the quantity
[[Green's Theorem]] uses.

## Reading it

Drop a tiny paddle wheel into the flow at that point. The curl points along the axis it spins about
(right-hand rule) and its magnitude is twice the angular speed. Zero curl means the paddle wheel
does not turn, which is **not** the same as the flow being straight: a shear flow with straight
parallel lines at different speeds has nonzero curl.

```
F = ⟨-y, x⟩         curl F = 2k          rigid rotation about the origin
F = ⟨x, y⟩          curl F = 0           pure source, no rotation
F = ⟨y, 0⟩          curl F = -k          straight parallel lines, still rotating
```

The third line is the one that catches people out and it is worth internalising: **curl measures
local spin, not global circulation of the picture.**

## The conservative test

$$
\nabla \times (\nabla f) = \mathbf{0}
$$

Curl of a [[Gradient]] is always zero, straight from Clairaut's theorem on mixed
[[Partial Derivative|partials]]. Run backwards on a **simply connected** domain it becomes a test:
curl-free implies the field is a gradient, so it is a [[Conservative Vector Field]] and its
[[Line Integral]] is path independent. The simple-connectedness condition is not decoration, and
the note on conservative fields carries the standard counterexample.

## Related

- [[Divergence]]: the other derivative, measuring spreading rather than spinning. Independent of
  this one; a field can have either, both, or neither
- [[Stokes' Theorem]]: the surface integral of the curl equals the circulation round the boundary,
  which is what makes curl the *density of circulation*
- [[Green's Theorem]]: the flat two-dimensional case of that
